verdicts.summary:
REVISE. There are three required changes; the decomposition itself stands. Do not change the component roster or the static relationships.

1. DynamicView uc9-drive-the-list-from-agent-tooling, step n4: this fragment misdescribes the design (Realization truth; Cross-Manager symmetry).
- The label "recordNewTodo / recordRewording / recordMarking / discardTodo / sweepCompleted(listOwner, change)", followed by the hop "keep the change", is a gross-terms placeholder for work that uc1-apply-a-list-change draws in full.
- It is also wrong on behavior. It shows every change going straight to one write. uc1 shows Mark All calling recallList first and then recordMarking (n15), a blank add writing nothing (n6), and a blank reword going to discardTodo (n10).
- The use case exists to promise Agents "the same List Behaviors a Team Member gets", so this chain cannot be the thinner one.
- Fix: redraw n4 at uc1's granularity. Name each behavior's verb and its TodoListAccess -> TodoListStore hop as step-local alternatives, include the recallList call before Mark All's recordMarking, and label the blank-Wording outcomes honestly.

2. TodoListAccess / Hosting-environment volatility: my ruling on the drafter's escalation.
- The doctrine gives each volatility exactly one disposition. This one is split between a typed claim on TodoListAccess and a deferral. It also contradicts the committed Hosting-environment rationale ("resolved by an operational concept rather than by a component") and the note on apply-a-list-change n24. The draft's own commit message says "The claim exists because of the gate."
- I am not asking you to drop the claim in this redraft. The drafter reports DH-VOL-ENCAP-MISSING reads only encapsulatesVolatilities and that waiver and disposition fields did not clear it. I did not re-run that experiment, and removing the claim would only repeat the same escalation. The scoped claim is at least true of this component: it does hold where the store is hosted and reached.
- What is wrong is that the exception is recorded only in a commit message. Fix: add an entry to .systemDesign waivers that names the exception, states that the claim is gate-driven, states that hosting is otherwise deferred to .operationalConcepts, and sets the re-evaluation trigger: drop the claim when the rule honors a deferral disposition. The human review gate must be able to see this on the artifact.

3. WebApp + WorkspaceEmbed / Presentation-host volatility: two components claim one volatility with no ratified facet group, and the live rules do not flag it. On the merits the split is right, because the committed rationale names two hosts from day one, so do not merge them. Fix: record the pair as one explicit facet group for ratification at the review gate (in the waivers entry or equivalent), and say so in each Client's Encapsulates prose within the 150-character limit.

Non-blocking comments (no response required; carry them forward):
- Change-propagation on ListManager: the claim is acceptable for today's pull mechanism. However, "a stronger mechanism would change the Manager" understates the effect, because push would also change both human Clients, and .operationalConcepts should say so. Reconciling simultaneous changes is not contained in the Manager: the stale-Todo guard sits at the store hop (uc10), and Mark All's recallList then recordMarking leaves a gap in which a concurrent add can land.
- The stale-Todo guard is drawn only in uc10 n4. The same verbs in uc1, uc4, uc5 and uc6 are the same calls but are labelled without the guard or its result. Align the labels if you are touching them; otherwise carry this into the TodoListAccess contract.
- Idempotency: every RA -> Resource hop cites the "caller's change id", but no Manager -> RA label passes it. The Manager must pass the key in, so the TodoListAccess contract needs it.
- ListManager is a domain-noun name that does not name the volatility it hides. With a single Manager this is not domain decomposition, so it is a naming comment only.
- DH-CARD-MANAGERS-MIN (Info): the single Manager is justified, since both core use cases share one sequence family and no committed volatility supports a second workflow. Record this in the D3 smallest-set attestation at standard check.
- DH-OBJ-COVERAGE (Warning, advisory) is open for objectives 1-5; resolve it in .operationalConcepts.
- IdentityProvider's dual role, as a Resource here and as the gateway authenticator in the prototype, remains for .operationalConcepts, as the drafter noted.
- The drafter reports .scrubbedRequirements reads as not committed, so B-NN traces are unchecked here too.

Checked with no defect: all 15 use cases have views with named titles; closed layering holds; a single Manager is entered in every view; zero Engines is consistent with the rejected variables (Filters, Mark All direction, Blank Wording, Outstanding Count) and within the 1:0-1 ratio; ListManager orchestrates rather than passing through; ResourceAccess verbs are business verbs; there are no queued or timer use cases, so trigger and delivery rules are not engaged; the draft commit made no change to the committed use cases, so no note was demoted; single-surface entries in uc9 and uc14 carry recorded justifications; uc4 n2 as a Client-only step is honest.

attempts.detail: the plan's cost was computed on ASSUMED values for the roster of roles, the working calendar, the agent rate card, the indirect daily rate, the declared load, the billing terms, the infrastructure kind, the normal option's staffing cap — the founder authored none, so these are the platform's documented defaults and not decisions

verdicts.summary:
REVISE. The two cores are sound and I ratify them: the count (2), the abstraction (nine brief items collapse under them), the rejection reasons, the variationOf links and the volatility coverage all pass, and the Hosting-environment exclusion is justified. Do not rework the core selection. Two defects must be fixed.

1. CHANNEL-SHAPED USE CASES. Two nonCore entries are delivery channels, and your own rejection reasons say so.
- "Drive the list from agent tooling": the n2 label is "Send a list change over MCP or the ordinary web API", and the reason says "A permutation of caller and protocol, not of behavior".
- "Work the list embedded in a Team Workspace": the reason says "A permutation of host, not of behavior".
Channels are permutations of one behavior and are never separate use cases, not even as variations. Each would also need its own dynamic view in architecture, restating the core chain.
Change: remove both as use cases. The customer's asks must stay visible, because they are objective 5 and the brief's delivery side. Carry them on the cores: Agent as a declared actor (already there), and Team Workspace and MCP/web API in the Machine-access protocol and Presentation-host seam notes (already partly there). State in the Apply a List Change and Take Stock of the List seam notes that these channels were folded in deliberately, so the raw ask keeps a trail. Also check that the Take Stock of the List note still covers the embedded case, including its Caller-identity crossing.

2. ACTORS AND LANES.
- The lane "Caller" appears in 12 of the 15 diagrams, including both cores, and resolves to no declared actor. It is not a glossary term either; the glossary's Who entries are Team Member, Agent and Team Workspace.
- "Team Workspace" is a lane on a use case that declares only Team Member (this goes away with item 1).
- On both cores, Agent is a declared actor that no lane or node represents: n2 is linked only to team-member, so the flow as drawn shows only a person. That undercuts the mission's "people and agents to one identical set of list behaviors".
Change: replace "Caller" with lanes named for the declared actors. In the cores, show the Agent's way in as well as the Team Member's. One option is a second start entry whose submit step merges before the "Establish whose Todo List" step, since multiple entries are legal; the mechanism is your call. "Todo Keeping" is acceptable as the system's area of interest and does not need to change. Apply the same lane fix to the variations, where the actor is only Team Member.

NON-BLOCKING (your call, not grounds for another round):
a. "Establish whose Todo List this caller may work" (n3 in both cores) has no outcome for a caller who cannot be mapped to a list, even though the glossary says a Todo List belongs to one person and is not shared. A flow crossing the Caller-identity seam should probably say what that caller gets.
b. The Take Stock of the List essenceRationale argues shared and immutable well, but its third leg argues "distinct from Apply a List Change" rather than differentiating. One sentence would close that, for example that demo apps' lists do not survive a service restart and do not give agents a true count.
c. "Look at the list on the caller's surface" and "Return attention to a list already open" read as human acts rather than system work. As actions they each carry a realization obligation; consider rewording them to the real request or making them notes.

BASIS NOTE: .mission, .glossary and .volatilities are staged, not committed, and no .scrubbedRequirements draft exists in project state. I critiqued against the staged slots and the research corpus. This does not count against this draft, but the Required Behaviors gap is still open.

todo-list-access.content:
# TodoListAccess: Requirements scope note

Activity: C-todo-list-access. Layer: ResourceAccess. Encapsulates Durable-storage technology volatility and the store's share of Hosting-environment volatility.

Trace notation: `ucN nM` is dynamic view N, activity node M, in the committed System. `rel` is a committed relationship. The verbs named here are the atomic business verbs already committed on the component. This note assigns no signatures or shapes to them.

## Purpose

TodoListAccess is the only way into the Lasting Record. It lets ListManager keep and recall a person's Todo List in business terms, and it keeps what the store is and where it runs out of sight of every other component.

## Responsibilities

1. **Record New Todo.** Lastingly keep a new Active Todo last in List Order. Trace: uc1 n7, uc3 n6.
2. **Record Rewording.** Lastingly keep one Todo's new Wording. Trace: uc1 n11, uc4 n8.
3. **Record Marking.** Lastingly keep one Todo's state (uc1 n14, uc6 n4), or every Todo's state as one act (uc1 n15, uc7 n5 and n6).
4. **Discard Todo.** Lastingly take one Todo off the list, including when a Commit Edit with blank Wording deletes it. Trace: uc1 n10 and n13, uc4 n7, uc5 n4.
5. **Sweep Completed.** Take every Completed Todo off the list as one act. Trace: uc1 n16, uc8 n4.
6. **Recall List.** Return the list as last kept: every Todo's Wording, state and place in List Order. Trace: uc1 n15 and n19, uc2 n4, uc3 n8, uc4 n10, uc5 n5, uc6 n5, uc7 n4 and n8, uc8 n5, uc9 n5, uc10 n9, uc11 n4, uc12 n4, uc13 n4, uc14 n4, uc15 n4.
7. **Stale-target handling.** Keep a rewording, marking or discard only if the Todo is still on the list, tell ListManager whether it was, and touch no other Todo. Trace: uc10 n4.
8. **Idempotent changes.** Honour the caller's change id on every change, so a repeated change has no second effect. Trace: rel todo-list-access to todo-list-store; every keep/take call in uc1, uc3 to uc10.
9. **Per-owner keeping.** Keep and recall each list under the listOwner ListManager supplies. Trace: the listOwner argument on every list-manager to todo-list-access call label; glossary Todo List.

## Not this component's job

No committed edge carries these to TodoListAccess, so they stay out of scope:

- Establishing or checking who the caller is: CallerAccess (uc1 n3).
- Filter Matching, Outstanding Counting and the Mark All Decision: worked out over Recall List by its caller (labels on uc2 n4, uc1 n19, uc7 n4).
- Blank Wording Check, and the Commit Edit or Cancel Edit decision: reached before any TodoListAccess call (uc4 n3, n7, n8).
- How changes reach other open views, and reconciling simultaneous changes: Change-propagation volatility, owned by ListManager.
- Presentation, protocols, and remembering the selected Filter.

Rejected in the committed Volatilities and not to be anticipated: extra Todo attributes, shared lists, undo/redo history, offline sync, manual reordering, reporting.

## Callers and consumers

- **Inbound:** ListManager only, synchronously (rel list-manager to todo-list-access). It is reached in all 15 dynamic views, always after CallerAccess has established the listOwner.
- **Outbound:** TodoListStore only, synchronously (rel todo-list-access to todo-list-store).
- **Not callers:** Clients never reach this component directly, and CallerAccess has no edge to it.
- **Queued and pub/sub:** every committed edge is sync, and the component has no event edges. See open question 7 about the missing operational concepts.

## Non-functional constraints

### Reliability (objectives 2 and 4, mission)

- **Durable before acknowledged.** A change reported as kept must survive a system restart or a store restart. The target is zero lost Todos, Wordings or states.
- **Read your own change.** A Recall List following a kept change must reflect that change, because ListManager builds the returned list and the Outstanding Count from it (uc3 n6 then n8), and that count must be correct 100% of the time.
- **All or nothing.** Mark every Todo and Sweep Completed never leave a partly applied list visible or kept (uc7 n5 and n6, uc8 n4).
- **Stable List Order.** Only a new Todo sets a place in List Order. Rewording, marking or removing another Todo does not move any Todo, and a repeated add creates no duplicate and no second place.
- **Quiet no-effect cases.** Sweep Completed with nothing Completed changes nothing and is not a failure (glossary Clear Completed). A person with nothing kept yet has an empty list, not a failure, so a first todo works unaided (objective 1).

### Maintainability

- Nothing about the store (technology, query language, keys, store errors, connection details) crosses to ListManager. Replacing the store must change only this component and its configuration.
- Failures must be distinguishable by whether a retry could help, since ListManager has to decide what to do with them.

### Extensibility

- The expected change is a replacement of the store or its hosting, with the zero-loss promise intact during any migration. Design for that change only.
- New Todo attributes and other rejected items are not extension points.

### Security

- **Isolation between people.** A call for one listOwner never reads or changes another person's list. A Todo id belonging to someone else behaves exactly like a Todo that is not on the list, and reveals nothing about it.
- **Trust boundary.** The listOwner is taken as established by CallerAccess via ListManager. This component does no authentication.
- **Wording is untrusted data.** It is free text that may come from Agents. It must be kept and returned exactly as given and never interpreted as a store instruction.
- **Store credentials.** They come from the environment and never appear in code, results or errors.

### Hosting

Endpoints, credentials and restart behaviour stay in configuration, so a move from team trial to sustained hosting needs no change to callers (Hosting-environment volatility).

## Full scope of the activity

The 10-day estimate has to cover more than the verbs:

- Learning curve on the chosen store.
- Integration with TodoListStore.
- A test client that exercises restart survival, repeated change ids, all-or-nothing behaviour, stale targets and isolation between owners against a real store, not an in-memory stand-in.
- The contract and documentation that C-list-manager builds against. C-list-manager depends on this activity.

## Open questions for Detailed Design

1. **Change id on the calling side.** The store edges carry the caller's change id, but the list-manager to todo-list-access call labels omit it. How does it reach this component?
2. **Change id lifetime.** How long must a change id be remembered, and is that record kept as durably as the change itself?
3. **Repeat versus stale.** A retried discard that already succeeded and a discard of a Todo removed elsewhere both find the Todo gone. Must they report differently? Answer against uc10 n4 and responsibility 8.
4. **Mark All race.** ListManager decides the direction from an earlier Recall List (uc7 n4), then marks every Todo. Does "every Todo" mean the list as kept at the moment of marking, including a Todo an Agent has just added? Who owns any resulting conflict: this component, or ListManager under Change-propagation volatility?
5. **Todo identity.** Where does a Todo's id originate, given that uc1 n7 and uc3 n6 pass no id?
6. **Defensive checks.** Wording is never blank on a Todo that exists, and that check sits upstream. Should this component also refuse blank Wording, or rely on its one caller?
7. **Missing basis artifacts.** The Deployment & Operations Model (slot 6) and Required Behaviors (slot 2) are not committed. So the store technology, its hosting, and the sync/queued and pub/sub map have no committed source, even though the component's description defers other hosting to an operational concept. This note relies on System edge modes and on the research corpus. The architect needs to name the store before the contract's retry and orchestration guidance can be final.
8. **No provisioning activity.** Nothing in the activity list provisions TodoListStore, and milestone M1 (Infrastructure Provisioned) has no dependencies. Does this activity own standing up the store, which the 10 days do not obviously include? The Manager or architect should decide.
9. **Latency and size bars.** No source sets a response time or a maximum list size. Usage growth was rejected as speculative, so no number is invented here. Detailed Design should state any working assumption explicitly, since Recall List returns the whole list on nearly every call.

CallerProof.description: Opaque proof of who is calling, as presented by the caller. Input to EstablishListOwner. Clients lift it unread from their own transport (WebApp session, WorkspaceEmbed host, MachineApi credential); ListManager forwards it unread. Only CallerAccess interprets it, and it verifies the proof against the IdentityProvider on every call, even when a front door has already authenticated the request. All caller kinds use this one type, so a new caller kind or identity scheme changes nothing outside this component. An Agent's proof must itself name the one person the Agent acts for, verifiably; no separate 'acting for' parameter exists, because a caller's own unverified claim never decides the owner. Handling: never retained after the call, and never written to logs, errors or traces. FOR ARCHITECT REVIEW: (1) the one-named-person rule for Agents is this design's decision, because no source says how an Agent maps to a person; (2) no source says what an MCP Apps host can supply, so uc14 depends on the host being able to present a proof of this kind.

EstablishmentFailure.description: Error model of EstablishListOwner. Any failure returns no ListOwner: there is no default, anonymous or guessed owner. callerNotEstablished is TERMINAL, do not retry: the proof is missing, malformed, expired or fails verification, it resolves to no person, or an Agent's proof names no one person. All of these return the same value, so the error reveals nothing about the identity scheme or why the proof failed; the caller must present a new proof. establishingUnavailable is TRANSIENT, safe to retry: the IdentityProvider could not be reached or could not answer, so nothing is known about the caller. It must never be reported as callerNotEstablished, and never be resolved by letting the caller through. Implement both as exported sentinel errors. FOR ARCHITECT REVIEW: the committed use cases and dynamic views have no path for either failure, so what the caller sees and how ListManager stops are not modelled. Recommendation: amend the use cases, stopping before any list work.

ListOwner.description: Opaque identifier of the one person whose Todo List this caller may work. Output of EstablishListOwner, the contract's only operation. ListManager passes it as listOwner on TodoListAccess calls; nobody may parse it or build one. Post-conditions: the same person gets the same value from every surface, and over time, because the value keys the Lasting Record. It is derived deterministically from the person's stable identifier at the IdentityProvider; CallerAccess holds no mapping store (no committed edge to one), and a first-time Team Member needs no setup step. Idempotency: read-only and safe to repeat, with no side effects on any list, so no idempotency key is needed. Behaviour: synchronous, called by ListManager before any list work; publishes and subscribes to no events. Retryability is declared on EstablishmentFailure. Orchestration guidance (advisory, a design estimate rather than a sourced figure): about 5 seconds per attempt; ListManager chooses the actual policy. App C 6.2a waiver: a single operation is deliberate, because the System commits one atomic business verb, all 15 dynamic views call only it, and TP-OP-REACHED forbids uncalled operations; padding would be designing to the metric. FOR ARCHITECT REVIEW: stability across a provider replacement requires the replacement to preserve this identifier; if it cannot, the System needs a mapping store.

ChangeID.description: Opaque caller-supplied idempotency token, stable across retries of one logical change and unique per logical change within a listOwner. Carries framework resourceaccess.IdempotencyKey semantics. Never empty.

ChangeOutcome.description: kept is false only when a change addressed one Todo that was not on this listOwner's list; nothing was changed in that case.

ListOwner.description: Opaque key of the person whose Todo List this is, as established by CallerAccess and passed by ListManager. Never empty.

TodoID.description: Opaque Todo identity minted by this component. Callers compare it for equality only.

TodoList.description: The list as last kept. The position of each entry in todos is its place in List Order. A person with nothing kept has an empty array.

Wording.description: Free text kept and returned byte for byte. Must be valid UTF-8 with no NUL character. Non-blank is the caller's precondition.

todoListAccess.notes:
# TodoListAccess: detailed design

Status: IN-DESIGN. Standard check complete; system-architect review is pending at the activity PR gate. Do not construct against this contract until that review passes. Designed to the senior-developer standard; reviewer: system-architect.

Facet: keep and recall one person's Todo List in the Lasting Record. One contract on this service. Caller: ListManager only, synchronous. No queued operations, no events, no Temporal.

## Operations

Every change takes changeId and is atomic and durable before it returns.

- RecordNewTodo: keeps a new Active Todo last in List Order and returns its minted TodoID. A repeat returns the same TodoID and creates nothing, even if that Todo has since changed or left the list.
- RecordRewording: keeps one Todo's new Wording. State and place do not change.
- RecordMarking: with todoId, keeps one Todo's state. With todoId absent, keeps the state of every Todo on the list at the moment of marking as one act, including a Todo added after the caller's last RecallList; kept is then always true, including on an empty list. Marking a Todo with the state it already has is kept=true.
- DiscardTodo: takes one Todo off the list. Other Todos keep their relative order.
- SweepCompleted: takes every Completed Todo off the list as one act. Nothing Completed is success with no change.
- RecallList: read-only. Returns the list as last kept, in List Order, and reflects every change already acknowledged. A person with nothing kept gets an empty list.

## Decisions on the scope note's open questions

1. Change id on the calling side: an explicit changeId parameter on all five change ops. The dynamic-view labels omit it, while the store edges already name it. ListManager derives it from workflowId:activityId, so a retry reuses it and a new logical change gets a new one.
2. Change id lifetime: the change and its recorded outcome commit in the same transaction, so they are equally durable. An outcome is remembered for at least 7 days, longer than any retry horizon; later pruning is internal.
3. Repeat versus stale: a repeat replays the first recorded outcome. A retried discard that succeeded reports kept=true. A discard with a new changeId of a Todo already gone reports kept=false, and a repeat of that change also reports kept=false.
4. Mark All race: the moment of marking defines every Todo, as in RecordMarking above. The direction decision and any resulting conflict belong to ListManager under Change-propagation volatility.
5. Todo identity: this component mints TodoID. Callers treat it as opaque.
6. Defensive checks: this component does not check for blank Wording. That rule sits upstream with the sole caller, and an access component holds no business rule. It refuses only Wording it could not return byte for byte: invalid UTF-8 or NUL.
9. Size and latency: no bar is set and no limit is enforced. Working assumption: lists are small, RecallList returns the whole list, and no paging is added because usage growth was rejected as speculative.

Open questions 7 and 8 need the architect; see Review questions.

## Idempotency

The dedup scope is (listOwner, changeId). Same changeId with the same change: first outcome returned, no second effect, and no List Order place consumed. Same changeId with a different change: Conflict, nothing changed. Store a fingerprint of the operation and arguments with the outcome to detect this. RecallList has no side effects.

## Error model

Use the framework resourceaccess.Error kinds. A Todo not on the list is never an error: it is kept=false.

- Transient, Infrastructure (retryable): store blip or store down. The change was not acknowledged; retry with the same changeId, which is safe even if it committed.
- Auth (terminal): store credentials refused.
- Conflict (terminal): changeId reused for a different change.
- ContractMisuse (terminal): empty listOwner, todoId or changeId; invalid state; Wording with invalid UTF-8 or NUL.

Store errors are wrapped and classified. No store detail, connection string, credential or other person's data reaches the Detail text or the caller. A malformed todoId is not misuse: it behaves as a Todo not on the list.

## Security

Every statement is scoped by listOwner. A TodoID belonging to someone else is indistinguishable from one not on the list (kept=false, no state change). This component does no authentication; it trusts listOwner from ListManager. Wording is bound only as a statement parameter, never interpolated. Credentials and endpoints come from the environment.

## Orchestration guidance (non-normative)

Advisory timeout: 5 seconds for RecallList, 10 seconds for changes. Retry only the retryable kinds and always with the same changeId. The caller picks the actual policy.

## Internal structure (for the constructor; not contract)

In package internal/resourceaccess/todolist: a Postgres store implementing TodoListAccess, built on framework-go-infrastructure-postgres, with reads and writes against the primary. Commit durably before acknowledging. Serialize changes per listOwner in one transaction so that List Order comes from a per-owner increasing sequence assigned only on a new Todo. Gaps are allowed and never exposed. The schema (Todos and the change ledger) belongs to this component, and migrations stay inside it. Test against a real Postgres via the testinfra container, covering restart survival, repeated changeIds, all-or-nothing behaviour, stale targets and isolation between owners.

## Factoring

The six ops are the committed atomic business verbs, each called by the dynamic views. Rejected: a separate mark-all op, because the committed views call recordMarking for both cases, and an absent todoId cannot express an invalid combination. Rejected: a generic applyChange, which would hide business verbs behind one op, and a read-one-Todo op, which no view calls. Rejected: returning a Todo snapshot from RecordNewTodo, which a replay could not honestly reproduce. Reuse test: a second team fronting a different store would implement this contract unchanged; nothing in it names the store.

## App C section 6 standard check

1 Reusable: PASS. 2a At least 2 ops: PASS. 2b 3 to 5 ops: WAIVED at 6 ops; the six verbs are committed on the System, are distinct business acts and all reached, and merging any would blur the facet. 2c At most 12: PASS. 2d Under 20: PASS. 3 No property-like ops: PASS. 4 At most 2 contracts: PASS (1). 5 Not a junior hand-off and 6 Architect or senior designer: PASS on the senior-developer default; state records no separate hand-off assignment, and the activity's junior-developer worker class applies to construction. Architect to confirm at review.

Layer rules: no queued ops, no events, no Temporal, one Resource behind it: PASS.

## Review questions for system-architect

- Store: Postgres is assumed because it is a sanctioned infrastructure option; the Deployment & Operations Model (slot 6) is not committed, so no source names the store. Confirm it.
- Provisioning: no activity provisions TodoListStore, and milestone M1 has no dependencies. Decide who stands it up. The design assumes this activity owns only the schema.
- Labels: list-manager to todo-list-access labels omit changeId. Confirm the parameter is enough, or amend the labels.
- Hand-off: confirm items 5 and 6 above.
todoListAccess.title: todoList contract

model.mission: Adopt the widely known TodoMVC behavior as a fixed contract rather than inventing a new experience, so there is nothing to learn. Treat every change as safely kept the moment it is made, and hold people and agents to one identical set of list behaviors wherever they reach it.

objectives.statement: Put the list into real daily use immediately: every team member records their first todo unaided within one minute of first opening it, with no training.
Earn trust that nothing is lost: zero todos, wordings, or done states are lost when someone leaves and returns, or when the system restarts.

Minimize the effort of keeping a list current: every correction, completion, or removal takes one deliberate action, no todo ever needs to be deleted and retyped, and clearing finished work or marking the whole list takes one step.
Give every member an accurate sense of what remains: the outstanding count is correct 100% of the time and visible at a glance, however they choose to review their list.
Let the team's agent tooling work alongside people: everything a person can do to a list, an agent can do with the same result, and the list is available in the places the team already works.

model.vision: A dependable personal todo list that a small team can start using from day one.

items.definition: A person on the small team who keeps a personal Todo List and works it by hand.
A member of the team's automated tooling that works a Todo List on the team's behalf, held to the same List Behaviors as a Team Member and getting the same results.
A place the team already works, other than the todo app itself, that presents the Todo List inside it so Team Members need not go elsewhere.
The one fixed set of things that can be done to a Todo List, identical for every Team Member and Agent wherever they reach it.
The widely known TodoMVC reference behavior, adopted unchanged as the exact definition of the List Behaviors so there is nothing new to learn.
One thing a Team Member wants to get done, made up of its Wording and whether it is Completed or Active.
The free text of a Todo that says what it is; never blank on a Todo that exists.
The state of a Todo that still has to be done; every Todo starts Active.
The state of a Todo that has been marked done; a Completed Todo stays on the list until removed.
The sequence of Todos on a Todo List, in the order they were added, with each new Todo placed last.
Put a new Active Todo at the end of the list from the Wording entered, leaving the entry empty and ready for the next one.
Deliberately change the Wording of an existing Todo without deleting and re-adding it, ending in either Commit Edit or Cancel Edit.
Finish an Edit Todo and keep the new Wording; if that Wording is blank the Todo is deleted instead.
Abandon an Edit Todo, discarding the change and restoring the original Wording.
Remove one Todo from the list, whether Active or Completed, without affecting any other Todo.
Change one Todo from Active to Completed or back again, without affecting any other Todo.
In one action, make every Todo Completed or, if every Todo is already Completed, make every Todo Active.
In one action, remove every Completed Todo from the list, leaving Active Todos untouched; has no effect when nothing is Completed.
A choice of which Todos to look at: All (every Todo), Active (only Active Todos), or Completed (only Completed Todos).
Switch among the Filters, always seeing which one is selected; this changes only what is shown, never any Todo.

Decide whether entered Wording is empty or only whitespace, so that a blank entry adds nothing and a blank edit deletes the Todo.
Determine from the list's overall state which way Mark All goes: to Active if every Todo is Completed, otherwise to Completed.
Determine which Todos belong under the selected Filter from whether each is Active or Completed.
Work out the Outstanding Count from every Todo on the list, regardless of the selected Filter.
Lastingly keep a newly added Todo at the end of the Todo List.
Lastingly keep the new Wording of one Todo.
Lastingly keep whether one Todo, or every Todo at once, is Active or Completed.
Lastingly take one Todo off the Todo List.
Lastingly take every Completed Todo off the Todo List as a single act.
Retrieve the Todo List as last kept, with every Todo's Wording, state, and place in the List Order.
The ordered collection of Todos kept for one person; it is not shared with other people.

items.name: Machine-access protocol volatility
items.rationale: WHAT: the protocols through which the team's agent tooling and other programs reach the List Behaviors (today an ordinary web API and MCP). WHY: longevity grounding — MCP shipped four dated specification revisions in roughly its first year (2024-11-05, 2025-03-26, 2025-06-18, 2025-11-25), and general-purpose web API conventions turn over more slowly but still do. At that rate several protocol revisions fall inside even a one-to-three-year system lifespan. RISK: likelihood is high, at least one breaking or material protocol change per year. Effect if unencapsulated: each revision ripples into the List Behaviors themselves, and web API and MCP callers drift apart, breaking the mission's promise that an Agent gets the same result as a person. Source basis: founder brief delivery paragraph; mission objective 5. B-NN traces pending: the Required Behaviors artifact did not exist when this was drafted.

items.name: Presentation-host volatility
items.rationale: WHAT: the hosts in which a Team Member sees and works the Todo List at the same moment: a standalone web app and an MCP Apps embedding inside a Team Workspace, each with its own lifecycle, input gestures, and sandbox limits. WHY: longevity grounding — web frontend technology has turned over every few years for over a decade (the founder's own reference point, TodoMVC, exists because frameworks keep replacing one another), and MCP Apps is newer and less settled still, so host changes fall inside a one-to-five-year lifespan. Which hosts matter also differs by Team Member today, depending on where each one works. RISK: likelihood is high, since two different hosts are required from day one and a new Team Workspace can arrive at any time. Effect if unencapsulated: list rules such as Mark All Decision and Filter Matching get reimplemented per host, the hosts disagree, and the Outstanding Count stops being reliably correct (objective 4). Source basis: founder brief delivery paragraph; mission objective 5; glossary Team Workspace. B-NN traces pending: the Required Behaviors artifact did not exist when this was drafted.

items.name: Caller-identity volatility
items.rationale: WHAT: how a caller is established and mapped to the Todo List it may work. Today this differs by caller type: a Team Member in a browser, a Team Member inside an embedding host, and an Agent acting on someone's behalf all prove who they are differently. WHY: the sources themselves are unsettled. The behavior reference says a single user/session, the glossary says one list per person, and the brief says a team, while the platform front door authenticates against an identity provider without saying how an Agent maps to a person's list. RISK: likelihood is high, because the question has to be answered for at least three kinds of caller at first release. Effect if unencapsulated: identity assumptions leak into every List Behavior and into the keying of the Lasting Record, so a change in the scheme forces edits and data migration across the whole system. Source basis: founder brief; behavior reference preamble; glossary Todo List and Agent; web-app deployment prototype. No longevity grounding is claimed; this entry needs B-NN traces once the Required Behaviors artifact exists.

items.name: Durable-storage technology volatility
items.rationale: WHAT: the technology and durability mechanism behind the Lasting Record. WHY: longevity grounding — a system that starts as a small-team trial commonly changes storage engine or hosted tier as use grows; as an architect's estimate rather than measured data, that is about once every few years, inside a three-to-five-year horizon, and the brief's 'start using tomorrow' favors a simple first choice that is likely to be outgrown. RISK: likelihood is moderate, perhaps one replacement over the system's life. Effect if unencapsulated: storage specifics leak into every list operation, and a replacement touches each one while objective 2's zero-loss promise is at stake during migration. Encapsulating behind business verbs (Record New Todo, Sweep Completed, Recall List) contains it. Source basis: reference section 9; mission objective 2; glossary Lasting Record. B-NN traces pending: the Required Behaviors artifact did not exist when this was drafted.

items.name: Change-propagation volatility
items.rationale: WHAT: how a change made by one actor reaches the other places the same Todo List is open, and how simultaneous changes are reconciled, for example an Agent clearing Completed Todos while a Team Member has the list open in a Team Workspace. WHY: the reference only requires the count to update after an action, which suffices for one person in one tab, but mission objectives 4 and 5 put people and agents on the same list across several hosts, and the acceptable answer (refresh on return, polling, pushed updates, conflict handling) will shift as agent use grows. RISK: likelihood is high once agents are in daily use, likely within the first year. Effect if unencapsulated: each host and each list operation embeds its own freshness and conflict assumptions, so moving to a stronger mechanism touches every Client and operation, and stale views show a wrong Outstanding Count. Source basis: reference section 8; mission objectives 4 and 5. No longevity grounding is claimed; this entry needs B-NN traces once the Required Behaviors artifact exists.

items.name: Hosting-environment volatility
items.rationale: WHAT: where and how the service runs, from a team trial to a sustained deployment under the house delivery standard. The platform doctrine fixes the runtime topology but leaves deployment scenario, scaling policy, and infrastructure building blocks as per-project choices. WHY: longevity grounding — the brief describes a team 'trying out' the app, so the move from trial to sustained use is expected within the first year, and hosting arrangements generally get revisited every few years (an architect's estimate, not measured data). RISK: likelihood is moderate to high for one move early on. Effect if unencapsulated: environment assumptions such as endpoints, credentials, and restart behavior spread through the Clients and the storage configuration, and a move risks the restart-survival promise of objective 2. This entry is expected to be resolved by an operational concept rather than by a component. Source basis: founder brief delivery paragraph; platform runtime doctrine; web-app deployment prototype. B-NN traces pending: the Required Behaviors artifact did not exist when this was drafted.

rejected.name: Todo attribute growth (due dates, priorities, tags)
rejected.reason: The behavior reference names exactly these as out of scope and says they must not be assumed required; nothing in the brief or mission signals demand for them.

rejected.name: Shared or team-wide lists
rejected.reason: The reference excludes multi-user sharing and the glossary defines a Todo List as not shared with other people; designing for it would serve a different product.

rejected.name: Undo/redo history
rejected.reason: Explicitly out of scope in the reference; Cancel Edit and the Mark Todo toggle already cover the reversals the brief asks for.

rejected.name: Offline use and sync
rejected.reason: Explicitly out of scope in the reference, and the mission places safekeeping in the Lasting Record rather than on a device.

rejected.name: Manual reordering of todos
rejected.reason: Drag-to-reorder is out of scope in the reference, and the glossary fixes List Order as the order Todos were added.

rejected.name: TodoMVC list-behavior rules changing
rejected.reason: The mission adopts TodoMVC as a fixed contract precisely so there is nothing to learn, and implementations share these rules identically; changing them would make this a different product.

rejected.name: Workflow-execution substrate
rejected.reason: Platform runtime doctrine fixes this for every system built here and already isolates it behind the MessageBus utility, so this project has no decision to encapsulate.

rejected.name: Set of Filters
rejected.reason: All, Active, and Completed are a closed set defined by the one state a Todo has, so a simple predicate handles them.

rejected.name: Blank Wording rule
rejected.reason: One whitespace test and a branch cover both the blank add and the blank edit-deletes-Todo cases.

rejected.name: Mark All direction
rejected.reason: A single conditional on whether every Todo is Completed fully decides the direction.

rejected.name: Outstanding Count calculation
rejected.reason: It is a count of Active Todos over the whole list with one definition; only its freshness across hosts can change, and that is covered by change-propagation volatility.

rejected.name: Remembering the selected Filter on return
rejected.reason: Whether the choice is kept is a small per-host setting that touches no Todo data and has no ripple effect.

rejected.name: Screen language and localization
rejected.reason: Wording is free text the user supplies, and no source mentions other languages; if labels ever needed translating, a string table would handle it.

rejected.name: Edit gestures (double-click, Enter, Escape, focus loss)
rejected.reason: Gestures differ only because hosts differ, so this is the same underlying change as Presentation-host volatility.

rejected.name: Web API consumer conventions
rejected.reason: Versioning and formats for programmatic callers change for the same reason as MCP revisions; folded into Machine-access protocol volatility.

rejected.name: Identity provider product
rejected.reason: Replacing the provider is one case of how callers are established, so it belongs to Caller-identity volatility.

rejected.name: Durability and backup guarantees
rejected.reason: Objective 2 fixes the promise at zero loss; how it is met changes with the storage mechanism, so it belongs to Durable-storage technology volatility.

rejected.name: Usage growth and load
rejected.reason: The brief describes a small team trying the app, and no source projects wider use; the platform's per-project scaling policy can cover a modest change without architectural seams.

rejected.name: Agent permissions differing from people's
rejected.reason: Objective 5 and the glossary require an Agent to do everything a person can with the same result; a restricted-agent policy has no support in the sources.

rejected.name: Reminders and notifications
rejected.reason: No source mentions alerting anyone; the Outstanding Count is the only awareness mechanism requested.

rejected.name: Reporting and analytics block
rejected.reason: A reflex block with no business volatility behind it: the only figure anyone asks for is the Outstanding Count.

rejected.name: Logging block
rejected.reason: A reflex block for this project: no source states a business need that would vary, and any operational logging belongs to the platform rather than to a volatility of this business.

rejected.name: Data residency and regulatory variation
rejected.reason: This is one internal team's tool with no stated market or regulatory spread, so no evidence supports designing for variation here.

decisions.essenceRationale: Every Team Member and Agent, on every host, comes for one thing: a change to their list that is kept the moment it is made and behaves the same for all of them. Six brief items (add, reword, remove, mark, mark all, sweep) are permutations of that single act and differ only in which List Behavior applies. It is nearly immutable: the mission fixes the TodoMVC contract, so protocols, hosts and storage can all be replaced while this flow stays the same. It is also what sets the product apart from the demo apps it is modeled on, which keep changes only in the browser and serve people only.

decisions.essenceRationale: Every member, whichever way they review their list, needs a true answer to what is on it and what remains. Objectives 2 and 4 are promises about exactly this: nothing is missing on return, and the Outstanding Count is right 100% of the time under any Filter. Returning, filtering, counting and catching up are permutations of the one act of reading the list as last kept. It is nearly immutable because it depends only on the Lasting Record and a closed set of Filters, and it stays stable as hosts and protocols change. It is distinct from Apply a List Change because it never alters a Todo, and without it a kept change gives no one any confidence: trust comes from seeing the list hold.
